strengths: The low-rank factor posterior is simple, broadly applicable, and produces substantial storage reductions across MLPs, LSTMs, and a small Transformer. The singular-support observation is mathematically correct and clearly distinguishes the induced weight distribution from a full-support mean-field Gaussian.

The empirical study covers several data modalities and includes useful baselines: deterministic networks, five-member deep ensembles, full-rank Bayes-by-Backprop, SVD initialization, and rank-one multiplicative perturbations. Multiple runs are reported for the main tasks.

The results show a potentially useful efficiency/quality trade-off. For example, the SST-2 low-rank model uses 1.5M parameters rather than 19.8M for full-rank BBB, while retaining reasonable accuracy and OOD performance; the reported Transformer training-time reduction is also practically relevant.

The paper is generally readable and unusually candid about calibration gaps, negligible small-model speedups, overlapping confidence intervals, rank/KL sensitivity, and missing comparisons. These honest limitations should not themselves be penalized.
The appendices contain extensive implementation details, initialization analysis, additional datasets, and derivations, making the intended method substantially clearer than the main text alone.
weaknesses: The central claim of provably tighter PAC-Bayes bounds is not established in general. The advertised parameter-count ratio requires the maximum per-coordinate KL to be equal between the full-rank and factorized posteriors. Using the same distributional family does not imply this: the learned posteriors, priors over functions, and even parameter spaces differ, and factor non-identifiability can substantially change KL. Without this unsupported equality, the theorem only gives a conditional criterion and does not show that the proposed posterior has a tighter bound.

The Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm bounds, whereas the method actually uses unbounded Gaussian factors without the proposed projection or truncation. The appendix sketches a high-probability alternative, but its bound involves a conditional predictor and extra assumptions and is not the theorem or empirical certificate presented in the main text. Consequently, this theory does not directly support the trained models.

The loss approximation results are elementary one-layer perturbation bounds around the truncated SVD of a full-rank optimum, rather than guarantees for the learned deep Bayesian network. The proof also incorrectly asserts that an expected-risk minimizer has no larger pointwise loss on every example. Although the final Lipschitz inequality can be repaired, the stated interpretation overreaches, and the observed singular-value decay is largely post-hoc.

The experimental comparisons do not substantiate several broad claims. Against deep ensembles, low-rank is materially worse on core predictive metrics on MIMIC-III (AUROC 0.895 versus 0.929; NLL 0.433 versus 0.300) and SST-2 (accuracy 0.806 versus 0.825; NLL 0.527 versus 0.434). Its advantage is concentrated in selected uncertainty metrics, often with overlapping uncertainty across only four or five runs.

Compute comparisons are incomplete. Bayesian predictions use 150–512 stochastic passes, whereas the ensemble uses five members, yet inference latency, FLOPs, and memory traffic are not reported. Parameter count alone therefore does not demonstrate cheaper uncertainty estimation, especially for deployment.

Rank and KL weight are chosen through ablations involving OOD/calibration trade-offs, but the manuscript does not identify separate OOD validation sets. This creates a serious possibility that the reported OOD test sets influenced model selection. The OOD benchmarks are also unusually easy shifts—adult ICU patients versus newborns and movie reviews versus news—and do not establish robust uncertainty quality under near-distribution shifts.

There are substantial reporting inconsistencies that undermine reproducibility: the Beijing split is 29,213/6,260/6,260 in the main text but 29,213/7,553/7,553 in the appendix; Table 2 reports four runs while Figure 6 says five; MIMIC parameter counts differ between the main table and appendix; and a PICP of 0.790 is described as near the nominal 0.95 level. The ECE protocol is also inconsistent about selecting the best binning configuration per model versus applying one configuration to all models.

The implementation description is extensive but no code or immutable artifact is provided, several dependency versions and data-splitting/extraction details are missing, and hyperparameter-search spaces and selection rules are not fully specified. Additional MNIST/Fashion-MNIST results appear to use only one training seed, so Monte Carlo forward passes do not establish run-to-run robustness.

The method itself—placing mean-field posteriors on low-rank factors—is a natural combination of standard matrix factorization and Bayes-by-Backprop. The singularity and parameter-count observations follow immediately from this construction. The breadth of implementation is valuable, but the methodological originality is modest relative to the paper's positioning.

The ethics discussion is inadequate for a paper using ICU mortality data and making safety-critical claims. It does not discuss data governance, subgroup performance, fairness, clinical deployment risks, or possible leakage from features such as length of stay. The generic impact statement is not commensurate with the clinical framing.

strengths: The core construction is simple and practically relevant: placing variational distributions on factors A and B reduces storage from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)) and can be used across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers.
The singular-support result is mathematically correct for r<min(m,n), and the covariance calculation usefully explains how independent factor distributions can induce dependencies among entries of W.

The empirical study covers three architecture families and reports multiple predictive, calibration, selective-prediction, OOD, parameter-count, and runtime measures over several seeds. The appendices contain substantial implementation and proof detail.
The experiments show genuine efficiency benefits, especially for the Transformer, and some promising OOD or selective-prediction results relative to full-rank BBB and rank-1 perturbations.

The manuscript is generally readable and openly acknowledges several limitations, including calibration degradation, overlapping confidence intervals, rank/KL tuning, limited architecture scale, and missing comparisons.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline claim of tighter PAC-Bayes guarantees is not established in general. The comparison replaces each KL by C_max times the parameter count and obtains the advertised ratio only by assuming equal per-parameter KL constants for two different parameterizations. Using the same distributional family does not imply this equality, particularly because AB^T is non-identifiable and its induced prior differs substantially from a direct prior on W. The general result merely states the condition under which the low-rank bound would be smaller.

Soundness: The Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm bounds on A and B, but the actual Gaussian variational posterior has unbounded support. Consequently, the theorem does not apply to the proposed implementation as stated. Later high-probability alternatives do not justify presenting the main result as a guarantee for the evaluated Gaussian BNN.

Soundness/significance: The Eckart-Young results concern a single linear map with bounded inputs, not the multilayer nonlinear networks evaluated in the paper. The learned-model bound leaves the uncontrolled quantity ||W-W_r^*||_F in the conclusion and is largely a triangle-inequality decomposition. Its proof also incorrectly claims that global optimality of expected loss implies pointwise loss optimality. These results do not support the broad claim of provable benefits for deep BNNs.

Empirical evidence: Several conclusions are overstated. On Beijing, the claimed coverage near the nominal 95% level is only 0.790, which remains severe undercoverage. Deep ensembles clearly outperform the method in predictive quality and often calibration, while the OOD gains are inconsistent across tasks. The paper offers only a hypothesis—not causal evidence—that singular geometry or induced correlations produce the observed OOD behavior.

Evaluation protocol: The ECE procedure searches multiple binning definitions and, in one appendix description, reports the lowest ECE separately for each model. This makes calibration comparisons optimistic and potentially incomparable. Rank and KL weights are also tuned through incompletely specified reduced-budget ablations, while arbitrary model- and task-specific KL scaling complicates interpretation as Bayesian inference.

Reproducibility/presentation: Important numerical descriptions conflict: the Beijing split is 29,213/6,260/6,260 in the main text but 29,213/7,553/7,553 in the appendix; its table says four runs while Figure 6 says five; and MIMIC parameter counts differ between the main table and appendix. No code or precise artifact-release statement is provided. Tables and plots are also very small, and radar plots obscure quantitative comparisons.

Originality: Low-rank factorization of Bayesian weights is a natural combination of variational Bayesian matrix factorization and low-rank neural parameterization. The singularity observation follows immediately from the rank constraint, while the approximation bounds are standard consequences of Eckart-Young and Lipschitz continuity. The related-work discussion does not convincingly establish that the conceptual contribution is as novel as claimed.

Scope and baselines: The main experiments use relatively small models and omit directly relevant alternatives such as SWAG and low-rank covariance VI, which the authors themselves acknowledge. Thus the claim that the method enables Bayesian inference for modern architectures or large-scale AI is not demonstrated.

Ethics/limitations: Although the paper motivates safety-critical and clinical use and evaluates ICU mortality, its impact statement says no consequences require discussion. It should address risks of unreliable uncertainty under demographic or institutional shift, the consequences of substantial miscalibration/undercoverage, and governance of MIMIC-derived clinical experiments. The honest technical limitations section is welcome, but it does not cover these deployment concerns.

The low-rank factor posterior is simple and practically useful: it reduces variational storage from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)) and induces structured row/column correlations despite factor-wise mean-field inference.

The empirical study covers classification, regression, time series, text, images, in-distribution prediction, calibration, OOD detection, and selective prediction. Results are reported over multiple seeds in the main experiments.

The parameter-efficiency results are compelling. For example, the SST-2 model uses 1.5M parameters versus 19.8M for full-rank BBB and 49.6M for a five-member ensemble, while retaining reasonably competitive accuracy and OOD performance.

The authors discuss important limitations candidly, including overlapping confidence intervals, calibration gaps, rank and KL-weight sensitivity, limited wall-clock gains at small scale, and missing comparisons. The singular-support result itself is correct and cleanly established.
weaknesses: The central claim of “provably tighter” PAC-Bayes bounds is not established generally. The comparison replaces each KL by a parameter-count upper bound and obtains the advertised ratio only by assuming equal maximum per-coordinate KL values across two differently parameterized, separately optimized posteriors. Using the same distributional family does not imply this equality. Thus the result is a conditional parameter-count argument, not evidence that the learned low-rank posterior has a tighter PAC-Bayes bound.

The Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm bounds on the sampled factors, but the implemented Gaussian posterior has unbounded support and the experiments do not use the projection, truncation, or modified analysis proposed in the appendix. Moreover, the theorem concerns the posterior-mean predictor rather than the full Bayesian predictive distribution. Its applicability to the reported method is therefore limited.

The approximation analysis is primarily a single linear-map truncation argument, not a guarantee for trained deep Bayesian networks. It compares a learned factorization with the truncated SVD of a full-rank optimum but does not control the stated learning-error term. There are also correctness/presentation inconsistencies: main-text Eq. (4) uses the sum of squared tail singular values where the appendix correctly uses its square root, and the proof of Theorem 3.6 incorrectly asserts that global optimality in expectation implies pointwise loss optimality.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate the source of the gains. A deterministic low-rank baseline is missing, so improvements cannot be attributed specifically to Bayesian factor uncertainty rather than rank-constrained capacity. Strong relevant alternatives such as SWAG, Laplace methods, and low-rank covariance posteriors are also absent, as the authors acknowledge.

Practical efficiency is evaluated mainly through parameter count and selected training times. Bayesian inference uses 150–512 stochastic forward passes, versus five passes for the ensemble, yet inference latency, FLOPs, and memory are not reported. This substantially weakens claims about efficient deployment.

Reproducibility is only partial: no code or artifact link is provided; exact rank-search spaces and validation criteria are unclear; KL temperatures vary substantially by task and are tuned for an unspecified balance of accuracy and uncertainty; and some reported details conflict. For example, the Beijing split sizes differ between the main text and appendix, its table and figure disagree on four versus five seeds, and MIMIC parameter counts differ between Tables 1 and 6. The heavily tempered objectives also should not simply be described as the standard ELBO.

Some evaluation choices risk optimistic or difficult-to-interpret conclusions. ECE configurations are selected inconsistently across sections, the MIMIC OOD population has a very different label prevalence, and several claimed advantages have overlapping error bars. Wider uncertainty intervals and high OOD scores are sometimes interpreted as more “reliable” or “safer” without demonstrating coverage conditional on clinically relevant subgroups or shifts.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than exceptional: applying Gaussian variational inference to low-rank factors is natural, while the singularity result follows directly from deterministic rank restriction. The work offers a useful empirical synthesis, but the current theoretical framing overstates what is novel and guaranteed. The generic impact statement is also inadequate given the paper’s repeated safety-critical and ICU-deployment motivation; risks of using OOD scores or uncertainty estimates in clinical decisions deserve explicit treatment.

strengths: The core construction is simple and practically useful: placing variational distributions on low-rank factors reduces storage from 2mn to 2r(m+n), and the experiments demonstrate substantial parameter and memory savings, especially for the SST-2 Transformer (1.47M parameters versus 19.84M for full-rank BBB).

The empirical study spans MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers, multiple prediction and uncertainty metrics, several seeds, rank ablations, controlled profiling, and comparisons with mean-field BBB, rank-1 perturbations, deep ensembles, and SWAG. The authors also report unfavorable results, including weaker in-domain NLL and the lack of consistent benefit from SVD initialization.

The measure-theoretic statement that the induced weight distribution is supported on the measure-zero rank-r set is correct for r<min(m,n), and the convex-hull argument provides an interesting route for relating posterior-mean predictors to deterministic low-rank function classes.

Presentation is generally organized and unusually detailed. The appendices specify architectures, preprocessing, seeds, priors, KL schedules, hardware, initialization, and Monte Carlo sample counts, and the limitations section candidly notes calibration gaps, overlapping intervals, rank/KL tuning, and missing comparisons.

The work has practical significance for memory-constrained uncertainty estimation: on SST-2 it retains competitive accuracy and OOD performance while materially reducing trainable parameters and peak GPU memory. No unresolved major ethical violation is apparent, and the use of established public benchmarks limits direct deployment risk.
weaknesses: The main PAC-Bayes claim is overstated. The advertised tighter-bound ratio follows only after assuming the maximum per-coordinate KL is equal for the low-rank and full-rank posteriors. Using the same distribution family does not imply this after learning, and factor scaling non-identifiability can substantially change the factor-space KL. Thus parameter count alone does not establish that the trained low-rank posterior has a tighter bound. Figure 3's empirical bound calculation is also insufficiently documented.

The main Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm-bounded factor support, whereas the implemented Gaussian variational posteriors have unbounded support and no clipping, truncation, or spectral normalization is used. The appendix gives high-probability alternatives, but these have extra convexity and tail terms and involve the conditional 'good' predictor; they are not the theorem stated in the main text or an evaluated certificate. Consequently, this guarantee does not directly apply to the reported models.

The Eckart-Young-Mirsky loss results concern a single linear map Wx, not the multilayer nonlinear MLPs, LSTMs, or Transformers used experimentally. They are mostly immediate Lipschitz consequences of matrix approximation and do not justify the broad claim of a network-level decomposition into optimization error and rank bias. The proof also incorrectly states that an expected-risk minimizer has no larger pointwise loss, although the displayed absolute-value bound could be repaired without that assertion.

The claimed uncertainty mechanism is not convincingly isolated. Under independent factor entries, distinct weights are correlated only in restricted cases such as sharing a row or column factor, and the covariance can vanish when the relevant factor means are zero. Lemma 3.5 therefore does not by itself support claims that singular geometry produces coherent uncertainty, prevents memorization, or explains the observed OOD results.

Rank and KL weight are said to be chosen by ablations balancing calibration and OOD performance, but the manuscript does not clearly identify separate OOD validation sets, selection criteria, or complete search spaces. Figures 10, 13, and 14 explicitly use OOD AUROC for selection; if the reported newborn/Guangzhou sets were also used for tuning, the headline OOD comparisons are test-set biased. This ambiguity materially affects reproducibility and evidential strength.

The evaluation lacks a rank-matched deterministic factorized network and equally budgeted low-rank ensemble, so improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to Bayesian factor uncertainty rather than low-rank regularization, capacity, or tuning. Broader modern uncertainty baselines are limited, and the paper itself acknowledges the missing low-rank-covariance comparison.

Efficiency is characterized mainly through stored parameters and training cost while Bayesian evaluation uses 150–512 stochastic passes, versus five members for deep ensembles. The appendix shows MC inference is expensive but does not provide a matched end-to-end inference latency or energy comparison. Claims of practical computational efficiency should therefore be restricted primarily to parameter memory and training in the largest experiment.

Some uncertainty comparisons are not fully controlled. Beijing's nominal 95% coverage is only 0.790 for the proposed model, and the description explicitly adds validation-residual noise for the deep ensemble without clearly stating an equivalent observation-noise treatment for every Bayesian method. OOD shifts are also coarse cross-domain choices, such as SST-2 versus AG News and adults versus newborns, rather than challenging near-OOD evaluations.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of an accompanying code or artifact statement despite a substantial custom implementation. Some choices are underspecified or potentially data-dependent, including ECE configuration selection and the derivation of Figure 3. The impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss credentialed MIMIC access, subgroup behavior, or the risks of interpreting benchmark OOD scores as clinical reliability.

strengths: The low-rank factor posterior is simple and potentially useful: it reduces trainable storage from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)), and the SST-2 profiling confirms substantial parameter and peak-memory savings.

The measure-theoretic result that the induced weight distribution is singular on the rank-at-most-r set is correct. The covariance calculation also identifies genuine row/column dependencies induced by shared factors.

The evaluation covers MLPs, LSTMs, and a small Transformer, generally uses 4–5 seeds, includes several uncertainty metrics, and compares against deterministic models, full-rank BBB, rank-1 perturbations, deep ensembles, and SWAG.

The discussion honestly acknowledges mixed results, overlapping confidence intervals, rank/KL sensitivity, weak wall-clock gains at smaller scales, and cases where deep ensembles or SWAG perform better. The extensive appendix gives useful architecture, optimization, prior, seed, and hardware details.

The manuscript is readable and logically organized, although very dense. weaknesses: The principal PAC-Bayes claim is not established for the learned models. The advertised sqrt(r(m+n)/mn) improvement assumes equal maximum per-parameter KL terms for the full- and low-rank posteriors. Using the same distributional families does not imply this equality after learning, and the paper does not empirically verify it. Thus parameter count alone does not prove a tighter bound. The numerical procedure behind Figure 3 is also insufficiently documented.

The Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm bounds on the factors, whereas the implemented Gaussian posteriors have unbounded support and apparently use neither truncation nor projection. The appendix derives a different high-probability result, requiring bounded convex loss and involving the conditional predictor f_good, but this is not the main stated theorem and is not connected quantitatively to the experiments. The displayed empirical Gaussian bounds are vacuous in any case.

The approximation theory is weakly connected to the proposed deep Bayesian method. The Eckart–Young loss results concern a single linear map and a fixed full-rank optimum; the Bayesian extension is a generic smoothness/variance inequality. It does not explain multilayer optimization or demonstrate that singular posterior geometry improves uncertainty. One proof also incorrectly states that optimality in expected risk implies pointwise loss dominance, although the expected-risk conclusion can be repaired without that step.

The singularity result is largely an immediate consequence of rank factorization, not evidence of a beneficial Bayesian mechanism. Claims such as preventing local memorization, enabling coherent uncertainty propagation, and causing the observed calibration/OOD behavior are asserted without controlled evidence. Under the stated mean-field factor posterior, off-diagonal weight covariances occur only for entries sharing a row or column and generally depend on nonzero factor means, so the presentation overstates the richness of the correlations.

Empirical gains are mixed and do not convincingly validate the central uncertainty claims. Deep ensembles are better on SST-2 accuracy, NLL, and OOD AUROC and on Beijing point prediction and OOD detection; on MIMIC the proposed method substantially worsens AUROC and NLL while improving uncertainty-ranking metrics. Several differences overlap across seeds, and no statistical tests are provided.

The OOD settings are all conspicuous domain shifts: adult versus newborn ICU records, sentiment versus news text, and different cities. MIMIC additionally changes mortality prevalence from 8.4% to 1.1% and includes age among the features. These tests do not establish robustness to subtle or clinically meaningful shifts, and they make it difficult to attribute detection performance to improved epistemic uncertainty.

Rank and KL weight are selected through vaguely described validation ablations targeting an accuracy–uncertainty tradeoff. The number of configurations, selection metric, and whether OOD data influenced selection are not reported, leaving substantial model-selection bias possible. SST-2 ECE is also chosen through a search over binning configurations, an unconventional procedure that is not adequately justified.

The efficiency comparison emphasizes stored parameters and training time while underplaying inference cost. The Bayesian evaluations use 150–512 Monte Carlo passes versus five ensemble members. The appendix itself reports roughly 32 seconds for MC100 on SST-2 versus about 0.23 seconds for one pass, yet matched end-to-end inference latency and energy comparisons are absent. This materially weakens claims of practical, resource-constrained uncertainty quantification.

Originality is modest: placing independent variational distributions on factors of W=AB^T is a direct combination of standard low-rank factorization and Bayes-by-Backprop. The singular-support observation and most theoretical components are elementary or transferred from existing results. Stronger comparisons with end-to-end low-rank covariance and other parameter-efficient Bayesian methods are explicitly left for future work.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix is detailed, but no code or artifact is supplied, several components are custom implementations, MIMIC preprocessing is nontrivial, and key procedures such as rank selection and Figure 3 bound computation remain underspecified.

The impact statement is perfunctory despite motivating the work through healthcare and safety-critical deployment. The paper should discuss risks from misleading uncertainty, subgroup performance, and the limitations of treating neonatal records as OOD. This is not by itself a decisive ethical violation, but it is inadequate treatment of the manuscript's deployment framing.

Overall, the paper contains a usable engineering idea and broad experiments, but the central theoretical advantages rely on assumptions not satisfied or verified by the implemented method, while the empirical results do not establish the claimed causal benefits of singular geometry. These are substantial soundness and evidential weaknesses rather than presentation-only issues.

strengths: The core idea is useful and practically motivated: placing variational distributions on low-rank factors reduces storage from O(mn) to O(r(m+n)) while enabling end-to-end Bayesian training without a pretrained backbone.

The empirical study is broad, covering MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on clinical, time-series, and text tasks. Results are reported over 4–5 seeds and include predictive performance, calibration, selective prediction, OOD detection, parameter counts, memory, and runtime.

The efficiency gains are convincing, especially for SST-2: the low-rank model uses 1.47M parameters versus 19.84M for full-rank BBB and 49.61M for a five-member ensemble, with corresponding memory and training-time reductions.

The manuscript clearly distinguishes factor-space inference from low-rank covariance approximations, Bayesian LoRA, rank-1 perturbations, and deterministic compression. The measure-theoretic singularity result is correct and provides a clean geometric characterization of the induced posterior.

Presentation is polished and unusually thorough. Assumptions, implementation details, initialization, additional baselines, rank sweeps, and negative results are documented extensively. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges overlapping confidence intervals, tuning requirements, modest small-model speedups, and weaker likelihood performance than ensembles.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are stronger than the results justify. The Eckart–Young–Mirsky loss bounds concern a single linear map and are essentially Lipschitz/triangle-inequality consequences; they do not establish analogous approximation guarantees for the nonlinear multilayer networks evaluated experimentally. Theorem 3.7 also leaves the central optimization error term uncontrolled.

The claim of provably tighter PAC-Bayes bounds relies on assuming comparable maximum per-coordinate KL values across two different parameterizations and induced priors. Parameter count alone does not establish this assumption, so the theorem gives a conditional scaling comparison rather than a general guarantee that the proposed posterior has a tighter bound.

The Gaussian-complexity theorem assumes almost-sure spectral-norm bounds, whereas the Gaussian variational posteriors used in the experiments have unbounded support and are not projected or truncated. The appendix discusses possible high-probability alternatives, but the primary theorem and empirical bound figure are not directly certificates for the implemented models; the reported empirical-bound computation is also insufficiently specified for reproduction.

The structured-correlation discussion is overstated. Under the stated fully factorized factor posterior, distinct weights have nonzero covariance only when they share an actual random A or B entry (the same row or column), and even those covariances can vanish for zero factor means. Thus the method does not generally induce covariance between every pair that merely uses the same latent index, and the manuscript does not establish that these particular correlations cause the observed uncertainty behavior.

Evaluation protocol creates potential selection bias. SST-2 development data are used for early stopping and then reported as the evaluation set. Rank and KL weight are selected through validation/ablation based partly on calibration–OOD tradeoffs, but no separate OOD validation set is described; the displayed MIMIC rank sweep appears to use the same newborn cohort later used for the headline OOD result. These choices make the strongest OOD comparisons less conclusive.

The OOD evaluations use relatively coarse shifts—adult versus newborn ICU records, SST-2 versus AG News, and Beijing versus Guangzhou—and therefore do not establish broad OOD robustness. Several headline gains are task-dependent, overlap in uncertainty across seeds, or trade substantially worse in-domain NLL for improved OOD scores.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite extensive prose: no code or artifact link is provided, several dependency versions are unspecified, rank-search budgets and selection rules are not fully enumerated, and the controlled profiling results use only one run. MIMIC-III additionally requires controlled data access and substantial preprocessing.

The use of newborn ICU records as an OOD cohort deserves an explicit ethics and subgroup discussion. Although MIMIC-III is de-identified, treating a clinically distinct vulnerable population primarily as distribution shift could mask label-prevalence and subgroup effects, and the manuscript's safety-oriented claims are not accompanied by subgroup or deployment-risk analysis.
